newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower before retail sales data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower before retail sales data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened lower on Tuesday as participants took profits and adjusted positions ahead of the government's June retail sales report.
The report, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, is expected to show that retail sales rose a slight 0.2 percent in June after a 0.1 percent decline in May.
Retail sales excluding auto transactions are believed to have revived moderately in June, rising 0.5 percent after slipping 0.1 percent in May.
At 0800 EDT/1200 GMT, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 8/32 to 100-21/32, yielding 6.56 percent.

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were up six basis points to 5.07 percent, six-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.12 percent and year bill rates were up two basis points to 5.26 percent.

"You saw some followthrough selling overnight and there was profit-taking ahead of the retail sales number this morning that is the key to the market today," said James Blumenthal, economist at MCM Moneywatch. "People took the opportunity to square their positions before the numbers."
Blumenthal said his firm is forecasting a 0.5 percent rise in June retail sales and a 0.8 percent gain excluding autos, a forecast that is higher than the consensus estimate.
"We see various factors contributing to a recovery from weakness in two prior months," he said.
Analysts said the market would look not only at the June retail sales number, but at the total picture for the second quarter, particularly at any revisions to May's 0.1 percent declines.
"Certainly with the retail sales number there's always the possibility or risk of a revision," said Blumenthal.
"The May retail sales number is frequently subject to an upward revision," he said.

The market is keenly interested in the retail sales data because investors and economists want to know if consumer demand is strengthening. Two-thirds of GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth is tied to consumer spending.
"Consumption is the main factor behind implications for Fed policy," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at Standard & Poor's MMS.
The question is whether June will offer any evidence of a pickup in spending following a very brisk first quarter and a slowdown in the first two months of the second quarter.

"We saw considerable weakness in the two months prior to June," said Rupert. "If the June number is strong and the prior months' figures are revised higher, the market might rethink its bullish posture and Fed-on-hold scenario.
"If we get a very strong number, the market will be hurt pretty badly," she said.
Rupert said prices were lower ahead of the retail sales report on position adjusting and a bit of profit-taking.
"European (debt) markets are lower," she noted.
Rumors circulated early that the seasonally adjusted BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index was up 0.9 percent in the week ended July 12 from the prior week.
Rupert said the rumor was not having a discernible impact.
"The market was already weaker (in early dealings)," she said.

Ten-year issues were down 6/32 to 102-16/32, yielding 6.28 percent. Five years were down 3/32 at 100-9/32 to yield 6.18 percent. Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-3/32, yielding 5.95 percent. -- (( N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
